تُظهر الأشرطة متوسط العمر بالأشهر (المقياس حتى 30 شهرًا). استنادًا إلى Cunningham (1982) في Newton (2004) ch.8. لاحظ اتساع المدى: فالمتوسطات تصف المجموعات لا الأفراد؛ والنمط هو تأخّر لا انحراف في التسلسل.

كيف تستخدم هذه المراحل

استخدمها لتفسير النمو لا للتنبؤ به. فهي تُظهر أن الفهم والإيماءة يسبقان الكلام عادةً، وهذا يسوّغ البدء المبكر بالإشارات والتواصل البصري. ويختلف الأطفال اختلافًا كبيرًا: فبعضهم يتكلم مبكرًا وبعضهم متأخرًا، وبعضهم يستخدم الإشارات أو الأجهزة سنوات طويلة.

وضوح الكلام: لماذا يجد الغرباء صعوبة في الفهم

المجموعة (Buckley & Sacks, 1986) نسبة ما يفهمه الوالدان عادةً نسبة ما يفهمه الغرباء عادةً
الفتيات دون 14 سنة 88% 45%
الفتيات فوق 14 سنة 86% 32%
الفتيان دون 14 سنة 86% 10%
الفتيان فوق 14 سنة 73% 18%

تذكر بيانات مسحية أخرى في الدليل أن كلام نحو أربعة من كل خمسة مراهقين يفهمه أفراد الأسرة بسهولة، بينما لا يفهم الغرباء بسهولة سوى نحو 30% من الفتيات و14% من الفتيان. ويعاني نحو 30% من البالغين من التأتأة أو التلعثم عرَضًا (مقابل نحو 1 من كل 20 صبيًّا عند دخول المدرسة في عموم السكان). Newton ch.6, ch.8, ch.9 ويُعدّ ضعف وضوح الكلام دافعًا رئيسيًا إلى العزلة الاجتماعية؛ فـ«كثير من هذه العزلة الاجتماعية ينشأ عن ضعف مهارات التواصل». Newton ch.9

الدلالة العملية: كل من يلتقي المتعلّم، من أقران وعاملي المقصف وسائقي الحافلات وأرباب العمل، يحتاج إلى استراتيجيات بسيطة للفهم، ويحتاج المتعلّم إلى قناة احتياطية (إشارات أو رموز أو كلمات مكتوبة أو جهاز).

مبادئ التدريس الصديق للتواصل

  1. بيئة غنية باللغة. التعلّم بين «أطفال آخرين أكثر كلامًا» وفي بيت وصف غنيّين باللغة يفيد اللغة «إفادة كبيرة». Newton ch.8
  2. انظر ثم قل. قدّم الكلمات مع الأشياء والصور والإشارات والمطبوع ليتوزع عبء الذاكرة اللفظية على عدة قنوات.
  3. قصير وواضح وملموس. بسّط التعليمات المنطوقة ليتمكن المتعلّم من ترديدها مصاحبةً للفعل («أمسِك، فوق، وادفع للداخل» عند ربط الأزرار). Newton ch.8
  4. انتظر. «امنح وقتًا إضافيًا للحصول على استجابة الطفل ومساهمته.» وشجّع بقية الصف على الصبر. Newton ch.8
  5. اقبل كل قناة. الإيماءة والإشارة والصورة والإشارة بالإصبع والكتابة ولوحة المفاتيح والإخراج الصوتي كلها تواصل.
  6. لا تفترض فهم اللغة الحرفية والمجازية. اشرح المصطلحات («أعلى الصفحة»، «كثير»، «أكثر»، «أولاً»، «أخيرًا»). Newton ch.8
  7. ركّز على المعنى أولاً ثم الشكل. أقرّ بالرسالة قبل تصحيح أصوات الكلام.
  8. أصغِ بعناية وكن صادقًا بشأن سوء الفهم. التظاهر بالفهم يعلّم المتعلّم أن التواصل يفشل.

الإجراء أ — بناء التواصل المبكر (من الولادة إلى المدرسة)

  1. أرسِ التواصل البصري والانتباه المشترك (الأشهر الثلاثة الأولى). يبدأ التواصل منذ الولادة؛ وفي نحو الشهر الثالث يردّ الرضّع الابتسامات عادةً. واللعب وجهًا لوجه والغناء والاستجابة للبكاء تبني الأساس. Newton ch.8
  2. استجب لكل محاولة. تعامل مع النظرات والأصوات ومدّ اليد والابتسامات على أنها أدوار في محادثة؛ انتظر ثم أجِب. فجودة التفاعل ودفؤه أهم من كثرته. Newton ch.5
  3. أدخل الإيماءات والإشارات مبكرًا جدًا (السنة الأولى أو الثانية). استخدم الإشارات المفتاحية مع الكلام: انطق الكلمة بوضوح وأدِّ إشارتها. فالإشارة «ستجنّب الطفل في الغالب الإحباط الناجم عن صعوبات التواصل». Newton ch.8 Chitty & Dawson ch.3
  4. استخدم الأشياء والصور والرموز لدعم الفهم والقراءة المبكرة (مثل رمز الكوب قبل وقت الشراب). Chitty & Dawson ch.3
  5. العب بالفم. الوجوه والأصوات والنفخ وألعاب اللسان والأناشيد القصيرة؛ انظر الإجراء ج.
  6. ابنِ المفردات عبر القراءة. شاركه الكتب يوميًا؛ سمِّ الصور؛ أضف الكلمة المكتوبة. «الطفل الذي يتعلّم حب الكتب هو في الغالب الطفل الأقل معاناة في التعرّف على الصور، ثم الكلمات لاحقًا.» Newton ch.8
  7. اجمع الكلمات. انتقل إلى عبارات من كلمتين وثلاث، معزَّزة بالكلمة المكتوبة. قدّم النموذج ووسّع: يقول الطفل «سيارة»؛ فتقول أنت «سيارة كبيرة… سيارة حمراء».
  8. أبقِ الإشارات والكلام معًا إلى أن يصبح الكلام واضحًا؛ ولا تُخفِ الإشارات تدريجيًا إلا عندما لا يعود المتعلّم بحاجة إليها.

عن الإشارة والكلام. يخشى بعض الآباء أن تثبّط الإشارة الكلام: «لا يوجد دليل يشير إلى أن هذه مشكلة. بل تشير الأدلة إلى أن الأطفال الذين يستخدمون لغة الإشارة أكثر احتمالاً لاستخدام الكلام من غير المشيرين.» Chitty & Dawson ch.3 وتحدد إرشادات DSi الإشارات المفتاحية بوصفها مقاربة فعّالة تدعم التواصل الأولي أثناء نمو الكلام. DSi §2.2.3

الأنظمة والأدوات

النظام / الأداة ما هو الاستخدام في التعليم ملاحظات
التواصل بالإشارات المفتاحية إشارة الكلمات المهمة فقط أثناء التحدث بجمل كاملة. المفردات المبكرة والتعليمات والروتين. مقاربة مدعومة بالأدلة في الإرشادات. DSi §2.2.3
ماكاتون برنامج لغوي يستخدم الإشارات (المشتقة من لغة الإشارة البريطانية) والرموز مع الكلام؛ بمستويات من التأسيسي إلى المعزَّز. الحضانة والمدرسة والبيت؛ ورش ودورات عن بُعد. مقرّه المملكة المتحدة. Chitty & Dawson ch.3
سيغنالونغ تواصل بالإشارات المفتاحية قائم على لغة الإشارة البريطانية، مع استخدام الإشارات دون تعديل حيثما أمكن. الأطفال ذوو صعوبات اللغة والتعلّم. Chitty & Dawson ch.3
الرموز وبطاقات الصور صور تمثّل كلمات أو أشياء أو أفعالاً. الجداول البصرية والاختيارات والقراءة المبكرة وكتب التواصل. Chitty & Dawson ch.3
كتاب / لوحة تواصل صفحة من الكلمات أو الرموز يشير إليها المتعلّم. اختيار الأشياء ومشاركة الأخبار والطلب. تركيب مهني
أنظمة تبادل الصور (مثل PECS) يسلّم المتعلّم صورة إلى شريكه ليطلب شيئًا. مفيدة حيث يكون الكلام ضئيلاً. تركيب مهني — غير وارد في المصادر؛ تحقّق من التدريب.
برمجيات تحويل النص إلى صوت وأجهزة توليد الكلام يُنطق بصوت عالٍ النص المكتوب أو المختار. العروض التقديمية والردود في الصف والحياة الراشدة. «برمجيات تحويل النص إلى صوت إلكترونيًا.» DSi §2.2.3
الحواسيب واللوحيات الكتابة والتسجيل والتصوير. الكتابة والتواصل والاستقلالية. تحقّق من حجم المؤشر وسرعته وتخطيط الشاشة. Newton ch.8

الإجراء ب — فهم الكلام غير الواضح (لكل راشد وقرين)

  1. أبطئ وامنح انتباهك الكامل. واجه المتحدث؛ وقلّل الضوضاء.
  2. أصغِ إلى الكلمة المفتاحية وإلى السياق (الموضوع، الأشياء، الصور، ما حدث للتو).
  3. أعِد ما فهمته («تريد الكتاب الأزرق؟»). أكِّد أو اطلب التصحيح.
  4. اطلب قناة أخرى: «أرني»، «هل تستطيع أن تشير بها؟»، «أشِر إليه»، «اكتبه».
  5. اعرض خيارين لتضييق الاحتمالات.
  6. استعن بدفتر التواصل بين البيت والمدرسة أو بالأسرة لفك رموز المواضيع المتكررة (اسم حيوان أليف، مكان).
  7. كن صادقًا إن ظللت لا تفهم: «لم أفهم بعد. لنحاول معًا»، وواصل المحاولة لاحقًا.
  8. لا تتظاهر أبدًا، ولا تُتمّم جمل المتعلّم عنه حين يكون قادرًا على إتمامها. تركيب مهني Newton ch.8

الإجراء ج — اللعب الفموي الحركي وألعاب أصوات الكلام

يؤثر انخفاض التوتر العضلي وعُسر الأداء الحركي في عضلات الكلام، ولذلك فإن «تمرين العضلات المرتبطة بالكلام قد يكون مفيدًا». ويقترح نيوتن ما يلي: Newton ch.8

  • ألعاب الأصوات: «ب، ب، ب» كقارب بمحرك؛ «س، س، س» كالأفعى؛ وأصوات الحيوانات والمركبات.
  • النفخ والمصّ: الشرب بالقشة؛ «كرة القدم بالنفخ»؛ الفقاعات والصفّارات والريش.
  • هاتف لعبة لتنمية استخدام الكلام والألفة به.
  • الأناشيد والأغاني: إن ترديد أناشيد الحضانة والملعب «سيزيد الطلاقة تدريجيًا ويعوّد الطفل على الإيقاعات الطبيعية للغة المنطوقة».
  • التحكم باللسان: إن أثر اللسان الكبير «ربما بُولغ فيه». وجهود إبقاء اللسان داخل الفم تنجح عادةً مع الصبر: إشارة سرية من العاملين في المدرسة، أو لعبة أو تذكير في البيت، أو المسح إلى الأسفل تحت الذقن. وأبقِ الأنف نظيفًا، فانسداد الأنف يشجّع على فتح الفم. Newton ch.5, ch.8
  • الجوقات ونوادي الخطابة موصى بها لتحسين الوضوح والطلاقة. DSi §2.2.3
  • علاج النطق واللغة حيثما توفّر، بالعمل مع الأسرة والمدرسة. DSi Rec 7

روتين لعب كلامي مدته خمس دقائق

حلقة الصباح: (1) «انفخ الريشة» عبر الطاولة—الشفتان مستديرتان؛ (2) «س-س-س» الأفعى و«ب-ب-ب» القارب بأسلوب النداء والجواب؛ (3) يغني الصف نشيدًا مألوفًا مع الحركات؛ (4) يختار المتعلّمون بطاقة صورة واحدة «يحكون» بها ما سيفعلونه في الاستراحة. يشارك الجميع—فهذا روتين شامل لا تدخّل لطفل واحد. تركيب مهني

الإجراء د — تعليم كلمة جديدة عبر عدة قنوات

  1. اعرض الشيء الحقيقي أو أدِّ الفعل؛ وانطق الكلمة مرة واحدة بوضوح.
  2. أضف الإشارة ودع المتعلّم يقلّدها (التقليد نقطة قوة).
  3. أضف الصورة والكلمة المطبوعة جنبًا إلى جنب؛ وأشِر إلى كل منهما.
  4. استخدمها في عبارة قصيرة («كلب كبير»، «أوقف السيارة») في نشاط حقيقي.
  5. تدرّب يوميًا في سياقات مختلفة لتتعمّم الكلمة.
  6. تحقّق من الفهم بالفعل («أعطني الكلب»)، لا بالترديد وحده.
  7. راجع على مدى عدة أيام؛ وأضفها إلى كتاب كلمات شخصي أو حلقة بطاقات.

القواعد النحوية والذاكرة والتسلسل

قد يستمر المتعلّمون في مواجهة صعوبة في اكتساب قواعد النحو؛ ومع ازدياد تعقّد الجمل، تضعهم صعوبات الذاكرة التسلسلية السمعية في موضع ضعف، ولذلك فإن «التركيز على مهارات التسلسل والذاكرة قد يساعد». Newton ch.8 ومن الطرق العملية:

  • اجعل القواعد مرئية: جمل مكتوبة بأجزاء ملوّنة؛ وبطاقات كلمات يمكن تحريكها.
  • أعِد الحكي بالصور بالترتيب؛ واستخدم خرائط القصة وشرائط الجمل.
  • علّم القراءة جنبًا إلى جنب مع الكلام: «سيسرّ المعلمين أن يعرفوا أن تعليم الأطفال القراءة يحسّن أيضًا مفاهيمهم اللغوية، ومن ثم كلامهم. فالكلمات التي يتعلّمون قراءتها هي الكلمات الأرجح ظهورًا في اللغة المنطوقة.» Newton ch.8

التكنولوجيا

«مع ظهور التكنولوجيا الحديثة، تتوفر فرص تعليمية ووسائل تواصل أكثر بكثير… غير أن هذه التكنولوجيا لا يمكنها حقًا أن تضاهي قيمة البيئة الغنية باللغة والتشجيع الحاني من الوالدين ومقدّمي الرعاية والمعلمين المهتمين.» Newton ch.8 استخدم الأجهزة أدواتٍ لا بدائل عن المحادثة. وشجّع استخدام الحواسيب «لتعزيز القدرة على التواصل بفعالية». DSi §2.2.5

التواصل مع الأسرة: دفتر التواصل بين البيت والمدرسة

للمتعلّمين الذين لا يستطيعون الإخبار عن يومهم، يسجّل دفتر التواصل بين البيت والمدرسة (أو ما يعادله رقميًا) الأحداث المهمة في الاتجاهين، ويوفّر موضوعات لوقت الأخبار و«يمكّنهم من المشاركة في أنشطة وقت القصة ووقت السجادة». ويجب أن يظل إيجابيًا، فـ«لا يتحول ببساطة إلى قائمة شكاوى». Newton ch.7–8

التواصل الاجتماعي والتوحّد

حيثما وُجدت صعوبات أوسع في التواصل الاجتماعي (يستوفي نحو 10–18% معايير التوحّد)، أضف بنية بصرية، وتعليمًا صريحًا لتبادل الأدوار والقواعد الاجتماعية، وأماكن هادئة، وروتينًا يمكن توقّعه؛ واطلب تقييمًا متخصصًا. DSi §2.2.3, Rec 8

تمرين 5.1 — خطّط لوقت حلقة صديق للتواصل

أنتِ معلمة في مرحلة الطفولة المبكرة. زين (4 سنوات) يفهم الطلبات البسيطة، ويستخدم ست إشارات وبضع كلمات، وكثيرًا ما لا يفهمه الأطفال الآخرون. خطّطي لحلقة مدتها 10 دقائق (أ) تدعم زين، و(ب) تفيد كل طفل، و(ج) تبني مهارات الكلام.

خطة ممكنة: (1) أغنية ترحيب بالأسماء، مع إشارة لكل طفل وبطاقة صورة (يتعلّم الجميع الإشارات؛ ويُظهر زين نقطة قوته). (2) جدول بصري لوقت الحلقة (أغنية – قصة – اختيار بطاقة). (3) قصة بالمجسّمات: ثلاث كلمات مفتاحية تُشار وتُنطق؛ صور على لوحة فلانيل؛ وتوقفات ليشير الأطفال أو ينطقوا الكلمة؛ وانتظار 5–10 ثوانٍ. (4) لعب كلامي: انفخي فقاعات و«فرقعيها» بصوت /ب/؛ وأفعى «س-س-س». (5) بطاقات اختيار («أي أغنية بعد ذلك؟») ليتواصل زين بالإشارة بالإصبع. (6) يتعلّم الأقران عبارتي «أرني» و«أشِر إليه» بوصفهما طريقتين عاديتين للمساعدة. روابط الأدلة: Chitty & Dawson ch.3 Newton ch.8 DSi §2.2.3, Recs 7, 10.

أهم النقاط

  • الفهم يفوق الكلام؛ امنح كل متعلّم قناة واحدة موثوقة على الأقل.
  • ابدأ بالإشارات والدعم البصري مبكرًا؛ فالأدلة تُظهر أن الإشارة لا تعيق الكلام.
  • استخدم اللعب الفموي الحركي والأناشيد والقراءة لتقوية عضلات الكلام واللغة.
  • علّم الجميع كيف يفهمون الكلام غير الواضح؛ ولا تتظاهر أبدًا بالفهم.
  • دعم التواصل مدى الحياة.
Core practice · 06

Literacy, Numeracy & Money

Reading as a relative strength, a staged route to literacy, maths at year level with tools, and teaching financial concepts.

≈ 6 min read1355 words

Why literacy and numeracy matter

“A major learning activity for children with Down syndrome in the primary years is the development of literacy skills, particularly learning to read… For many children, reading is a relative strength and serves an important foundation when learning to read is replaced by reading to learn.” DSi §5.2.1 Reading supports speech, friendships and social inclusion across life, and “the importance of literacy development for friendship and other areas of social inclusion imply the detriment caused if opportunities are not available for continuing literacy learning.” DSi §5.3.3 Secondary students in mainstream classes made significant gains in expressive language and literacy compared with special-school peers. DSi §5.2.2

Reading: the evidence-informed route

Most children “will be able to read and write when they are older. They should be encouraged to explore books from an early age.” Occasionally a child has greater difficulty, which should be discussed with the teacher and support staff; “final success in reading will vary greatly.” Newton ch.8 Strengths to use: visual memory, whole-word recognition, picture support; challenges to plan around: phonological awareness, verbal memory, speech clarity, and hearing. DSi §2.2.3

Procedure: staged literacy teaching Synthesis

  1. Share books daily from infancy. Look at pictures, name them, turn pages, repeat favourites; link to signs and real objects. Newton ch.8
  2. Build a sight vocabulary of single words. Start with the child’s name, family, favourite things and classroom labels; match word to word, then word to picture; keep 5–10 words active and review often. “Children should be encouraged to build up sight vocabulary of single words.” Newton ch.8 Sight vocabulary
  3. Move from words to phrases and sentences. Two- and three-word phrases (“big dog”), then simple sentences, using word cards that can be rearranged to show grammar.
  4. Link reading to speech. Read words aloud together; the words learned to read are those most likely to appear in spoken language. Newton ch.8
  5. Add sound awareness gradually. Teach rhymes, syllable clapping and initial sounds through games and songs while continuing whole-word reading; check hearing first. DSi §2.2.3 Synthesis
  6. Use books of interest and age-appropriate texts. Teenagers and adults need “developmentally and socially appropriate literacy activities”; popular-culture texts are effective. DSi §5.2.2, §5.3.3
  7. Teach reading to learn. Use picture-supported, shortened or audio versions of curriculum texts so content learning is not blocked by decoding speed. DSi §5.2.2
  8. Teach directionality and strategies explicitly. Adults may read words “at random when the text was difficult”; keep reminding left-to-right and finger-tracking. DSi §5.3.3
  9. Write in the way that works. Keyboard, tablet, voice-to-text, tracing and copying all count; keep handwriting practice short and purposeful. DSi §2.2.5

A one-week sight-word cycle

Monday: introduce 3 new words with objects and signs. Tuesday: matching games (word-word, word-picture). Wednesday: find the word in a sentence strip. Thursday: use the word in a short written sentence on a keyboard. Friday: review all previous words as a game; send home the word cards. Add one new word only after the last is secure. Synthesis

Writing and fine motor access

Fine-motor limits should not cap composition. Provide footrests, slanted writing surfaces, grips, large-ruled paper, trainer scissors and a computer option; teach typing early; separate composing from handwriting. Newton ch.8 DSi §2.2.5, Rec 12 “Although learners will continue to develop handwriting and drawing skills throughout their lives, encouraging the use of computers will enhance the ability to communicate effectively.” DSi §2.2.5

Numeracy and mathematics

Mathematics has produced “remarkable results” when the year-level curriculum is adjusted: learners who had not shown mastery of simple arithmetic achieved goals in algebra and trigonometry—with calculators as needed. DSi §4.2.1 Before moving to addition, “it is useful to check a child’s grasp of numbers.” Newton ch.8

Procedure: teaching a maths concept at year level Synthesis

  1. State the year-level concept (e.g. fractions, area, linear equations).
  2. Check prerequisites visually and concretely: number sense, one-to-one counting, number line, place-value materials.
  3. Make the concept concrete: objects, folding paper, cubes, measuring, money, food, tiles.
  4. Use a number line, grid or chart on the desk and a calculator for computation so working memory is available for reasoning. DSi §4.2.2
  5. Provide enabling prompts: a worked example, a partly completed table, a first step done. Offer only when the learner signals the need. DSi §4.2.1
  6. Provide extending prompts: “What if…?” questions, patterns, real-life problems.
  7. Teach vocabulary explicitly: “more”, “less”, “first”, “last”, “top”—these may be interpreted literally. Newton ch.8
  8. Assess by doing and explaining with materials, not only by writing.

Learning beyond basic arithmetic

Faragher (2014), Monari Martinez (1998) and Monari Martinez & Pellegrini (2010) are cited in the Guidelines for learners with Down syndrome achieving algebra and trigonometry goals with support; the key adjustment was the use of calculators. DSi §4.2.1

Financial literacy and life numeracy

The Guidelines point out that old skills such as counting coins and calculating change matter less where payments are electronic. “Of critical importance are overarching concepts such as budgeting, saving, spending, earning interest and borrowing money. These should be taught as concepts, rather than relying on specific techniques that may become outdated.” Tools—teller machines, online banking, spreadsheets—remove calculation barriers. DSi §5.3.3

Concept Teaching idea Tool
Earning Link pay to hours and tasks; payslip reading with pictures Visual payslip, calendar
Spending “Wants vs needs” sorting; comparing prices; checking a receipt Phone camera, price cards
Saving Goal chart with picture of the item; weekly progress Savings app, jar, spreadsheet
Budgeting Three-column budget (must pay / choose / save) Spreadsheet template with colours
Borrowing and interest Simple stories: borrowing from friend vs loan; risks Role play, short videos
Safety Never share PINs; check with a trusted person before big spending Wallet card with “Stop—Ask”

People with Down syndrome “are vulnerable to financial abuse”; strategies include more than one trusted advisor overseeing expenditure and a supported decision-making model. DSi §5.3.3, Rec 46

Numeracy in daily life

Numeracy “may require explicit planning… because opportunities to do so vicariously may be limited.” DSi §5.3.3 Build it into cooking (measuring), travel (timetables), phone use (calendar, timers), shopping (budget), sport (scores). Teach in the real context, as the need arises.

Time, money and “literal” concepts

Because time concepts are weak, explain when events occur using accurate, concrete markers (“after lunch”) and visual timetables; ensure the activity you name really is the last one before home time. Newton ch.7

Exercise 6.1 — Adjust a Year 8 maths lesson on percentages

Learning intention: calculate a percentage of an amount. The class will do 12 questions on a worksheet. Ravi has Down syndrome, reads simple sentences, and uses a calculator.

Task: Design (a) the concrete introduction, (b) the supports, (c) an enabling prompt, (d) an extending prompt and (e) how you will assess.

(a) Real-life sale scene: price tags showing 10%, 25%, 50% off; cut a chocolate bar into tenths, quarters and halves. (b) Percentage-fraction-decimal chart on the desk; calculator; coloured grid showing 100 squares; sentence frame “10% of ___ is ___.” (c) Enabling prompt: a worked example with the first line completed, or a partially filled table, offered when he pauses. (d) Extending prompt: “Which is cheaper: 25% off £40 or 10% off £30?” or comparing two shops. (e) Observe him find 10% of three prices using the grid and calculator and explain choices orally or by showing; record on the lesson sheet. Keep the Year 8 outcome, reduce the number of items and use the tools. DSi §4.2.1–4.2.2, Rec 25

Key takeaways

  • Reading is a relative strength: teach with sight words, books, pictures and real purposes.
  • Connect reading to speech; use technology for writing.
  • Teach maths at year level with concrete materials, charts and calculators.
  • Teach financial concepts, not outdated techniques; protect against abuse with trusted advisers.
الممارسة الأساسية · 06

القراءة والكتابة والحساب والمال

القراءة نقطة قوة نسبية، ومسار متدرج لتعلّم القراءة، والرياضيات على مستوى الصف مع الأدوات، وتعليم المفاهيم المالية.

≈ 7 دقيقة قراءة1436 كلمة

لماذا تهمّ القراءة والكتابة والحساب

“من الأنشطة التعلّمية الرئيسة لدى الأطفال ذوي متلازمة داون في سنوات المرحلة الابتدائية تنمية مهارات القراءة والكتابة، ولا سيما تعلّم القراءة… وبالنسبة لكثير من الأطفال تمثل القراءة نقطة قوة نسبية وأساسًا مهمًا عندما يحلّ ‘القراءة للتعلّم’ محل ‘تعلّم القراءة’.” DSi §5.2.1 وتدعم القراءة الكلام والصداقات والدمج الاجتماعي طوال الحياة، و“إن أهمية تنمية مهارات القراءة والكتابة للصداقة ولسائر مجالات الدمج الاجتماعي تعني الضرر الذي يلحق بالفرد إذا لم تتوافر فرص لمواصلة تعلّم القراءة والكتابة.” DSi §5.3.3 وقد حقق طلبة المرحلة الثانوية في الصفوف العادية مكاسب كبيرة في اللغة التعبيرية والقراءة والكتابة مقارنة بأقرانهم في المدارس الخاصة. DSi §5.2.2

القراءة: المسار المستنير بالأدلة

“سيكون معظم الأطفال قادرين على القراءة والكتابة عندما يكبرون. وينبغي تشجيعهم على استكشاف الكتب منذ سن مبكرة.” وأحيانًا يواجه الطفل صعوبة أكبر، وينبغي مناقشة ذلك مع المعلم والعاملين الداعمين؛ و“سيتفاوت النجاح النهائي في القراءة تفاوتًا كبيرًا.” Newton ch.8 جوانب القوة التي ينبغي توظيفها: الذاكرة البصرية، والتعرّف على الكلمة كاملةً، والدعم بالصور؛ والتحديات التي ينبغي التخطيط لها: الوعي الصوتي، والذاكرة اللفظية، ووضوح الكلام، والسمع. DSi §2.2.3

إجراء: تدريس القراءة والكتابة على مراحل تركيب مهني

  1. شارك الكتب يوميًا منذ الرضاعة. انظروا إلى الصور وسمّوها، وقلّبوا الصفحات، وأعيدوا الكتب المفضلة؛ واربطوا ذلك بالإشارات والأشياء الحقيقية. Newton ch.8
  2. ابنِ مفردات بصرية من الكلمات المفردة. ابدأ باسم الطفل وأسرته وأشيائه المفضلة وملصقات الصف؛ طابِق الكلمة بالكلمة، ثم الكلمة بالصورة؛ وأبقِ 5–10 كلمات نشطة وراجعها كثيرًا. “ينبغي تشجيع الأطفال على بناء مفردات بصرية من الكلمات المفردة.” Newton ch.8 المفردات البصرية
  3. انتقل من الكلمات إلى العبارات والجمل. عبارات من كلمتين وثلاث كلمات (“big dog”، أي «كلب كبير»)، ثم جمل بسيطة، باستخدام بطاقات كلمات يمكن إعادة ترتيبها لإظهار القواعد. (يبقى المثال بالإنجليزية لأن الهدف تدريب الطفل على قراءة الكلمات الإنجليزية؛ ويُكيَّف بمفردات اللغة المستخدمة في صفك.)
  4. اربط القراءة بالكلام. اقرؤوا الكلمات بصوت عالٍ معًا؛ فالكلمات التي يتعلّم الطفل قراءتها هي الأكثر احتمالًا للظهور في كلامه المنطوق. Newton ch.8
  5. أضِف الوعي بالأصوات تدريجيًا. علّم القوافي، وتقطيع المقاطع بالتصفيق، والأصوات الأولى من خلال الألعاب والأغاني مع مواصلة قراءة الكلمة كاملةً؛ وتحقق من السمع أولًا. DSi §2.2.3 تركيب مهني
  6. استخدم كتبًا تثير الاهتمام ونصوصًا مناسبة للعمر. يحتاج المراهقون والكبار إلى “أنشطة قرائية وكتابية مناسبة نمائيًا واجتماعيًا”؛ وتُعدّ النصوص المستمدة من الثقافة الشعبية فعّالة. DSi §5.2.2, §5.3.3
  7. علّم القراءة للتعلّم. استخدم نسخًا من نصوص المنهج مدعومة بالصور أو مختصرة أو صوتية بحيث لا يُعيق بطء فك الرموز تعلّمَ المحتوى. DSi §5.2.2
  8. علّم الاتجاهية والاستراتيجيات بوضوح. قد يقرأ الكبار الكلمات “عشوائيًا عندما يكون النص صعبًا”؛ فواصل التذكير بالقراءة من اليسار إلى اليمين (في الإنجليزية) وبتتبّع الكلمات بالإصبع. DSi §5.3.3
  9. اكتب بالطريقة التي تناسب المتعلّم. تُحتسب لوحة المفاتيح والجهاز اللوحي والتحويل من الصوت إلى نص والتتبّع والنسخ جميعها؛ واجعل تدريب الخط قصيرًا وهادفًا. DSi §2.2.5

دورة أسبوعية لتعلّم الكلمات البصرية

الاثنين: قدّم 3 كلمات جديدة مع أشياء وإشارات. الثلاثاء: ألعاب مطابقة (كلمة بكلمة، وكلمة بصورة). الأربعاء: العثور على الكلمة في شريط جملة. الخميس: استخدام الكلمة في جملة مكتوبة قصيرة على لوحة المفاتيح. الجمعة: مراجعة جميع الكلمات السابقة على شكل لعبة؛ وإرسال بطاقات الكلمات إلى المنزل. لا تضف كلمة جديدة إلا بعد أن تترسّخ الكلمة السابقة. تركيب مهني

الكتابة وتيسير الوصول لذوي المهارات الحركية الدقيقة

ينبغي ألا تضع محدودية المهارات الحركية الدقيقة سقفًا للتعبير الكتابي. وفّر مساند للقدمين، وأسطح كتابة مائلة، ومقابض للأقلام، وورقًا بأسطر عريضة، ومقصات تدريبية، وخيار الحاسوب؛ وعلّم الطباعة مبكرًا؛ وافصل بين التأليف والكتابة اليدوية. Newton ch.8 DSi §2.2.5, Rec 12 “ورغم أن المتعلّمين سيواصلون تنمية مهارات الكتابة اليدوية والرسم طوال حياتهم، فإن تشجيع استخدام الحواسيب سيعزّز القدرة على التواصل بفاعلية.” DSi §2.2.5

الحساب والرياضيات

حققت الرياضيات “نتائج لافتة” عندما يتم تكييف منهج الصف (المرحلة الدراسية): فقد بلغ متعلّمون لم يُظهروا إتقانًا للحساب البسيط أهدافًا في الجبر وحساب المثلثات، مع استخدام الآلات الحاسبة عند الحاجة. DSi §4.2.1 وقبل الانتقال إلى الجمع، “من المفيد التحقق من فهم الطفل للأعداد.” Newton ch.8

إجراء: تدريس مفهوم رياضي على مستوى الصف تركيب مهني

  1. حدّد المفهوم المطلوب على مستوى الصف (مثل الكسور، والمساحة، والمعادلات الخطية).
  2. تحقق من المتطلبات السابقة بصريًا وحسّيًا: الحس العددي، والعد بمقابلة واحد لواحد، وخط الأعداد، ومواد القيمة المنزلية.
  3. اجعل المفهوم محسوسًا: أشياء، وطيّ الورق، ومكعبات، وقياس، ونقود، وطعام، وبلاط.
  4. استخدم خط أعداد أو شبكة أو مخططًا على المكتب وآلة حاسبة للحساب بحيث تتوافر الذاكرة العاملة للاستدلال. DSi §4.2.2
  5. قدّم تلميحات ميسِّرة: مثال محلول، أو جدول مكتمل جزئيًا، أو خطوة أولى مُنجزة. لا تقدّمها إلا عندما يشير المتعلّم إلى حاجته إليها. DSi §4.2.1
  6. قدّم تلميحات إثرائية: أسئلة “ماذا لو…؟”، وأنماط، ومسائل من الحياة الواقعية.
  7. علّم المفردات بوضوح: “أكثر”، و“أقل”، و“أولًا”، و“أخيرًا”، و“أعلى”، فقد تُفهم حرفيًا. Newton ch.8
  8. قيّم بالعمل والشرح باستخدام المواد المحسوسة، لا بالكتابة وحدها.

التعلّم إلى ما بعد الحساب الأساسي

يستشهد الدليل الإرشادي بكل من Faragher (2014) وMonari Martinez (1998) وMonari Martinez & Pellegrini (2010) في شأن متعلّمين ذوي متلازمة داون بلغوا أهدافًا في الجبر وحساب المثلثات بالدعم؛ وكان التعديل الأساسي هو استخدام الآلات الحاسبة. DSi §4.2.1

الثقافة المالية والحساب في الحياة اليومية

يشير الدليل الإرشادي إلى أن المهارات القديمة مثل عدّ العملات المعدنية وحساب الباقي أقل أهمية حيث تكون المدفوعات إلكترونية. “الأهمية الحاسمة تكمن في المفاهيم الشاملة مثل وضع الميزانية، والادخار، والإنفاق، وكسب الفائدة، واقتراض المال. وينبغي تدريس هذه المفاهيم بوصفها مفاهيم، لا الاعتماد على تقنيات محددة قد تصبح قديمة.” وتزيل أدوات مثل أجهزة الصرّاف الآلي والخدمات المصرفية عبر الإنترنت والجداول الإلكترونية عوائق الحساب. DSi §5.3.3

المفهوم فكرة للتدريس الأداة
الكسب ربط الأجر بالساعات والمهام؛ وقراءة كشف الراتب بالصور كشف راتب مصوَّر، وتقويم
الإنفاق فرز “الرغبات مقابل الحاجات”؛ ومقارنة الأسعار؛ وفحص الإيصال كاميرا الهاتف، وبطاقات الأسعار
الادخار مخطط هدف بصورة للسلعة؛ وتقدّم أسبوعي تطبيق ادخار، وحصّالة، وجدول إلكتروني
وضع الميزانية ميزانية من ثلاثة أعمدة (واجب الدفع / اختياري / ادخار) قالب جدول إلكتروني ملوَّن
الاقتراض والفائدة قصص بسيطة: الاقتراض من صديق مقابل القرض؛ والمخاطر لعب الأدوار، ومقاطع فيديو قصيرة
السلامة عدم مشاركة الأرقام السرية؛ واستشارة شخص موثوق قبل الإنفاق الكبير بطاقة محفظة بعبارة “قف — اسأل”

إن الأشخاص ذوي متلازمة داون “عرضة للاستغلال المالي”؛ وتشمل الاستراتيجيات أكثر من مستشار موثوق يشرف على الإنفاق ونموذج اتخاذ القرار المدعوم. DSi §5.3.3, Rec 46

الحساب في الحياة اليومية

قد يتطلب الحساب “تخطيطًا صريحًا… لأن فرص تعلّمه بالمشاهدة غير المباشرة قد تكون محدودة.” DSi §5.3.3 أدمجه في الطهي (القياس)، والسفر (جداول المواعيد)، واستخدام الهاتف (التقويم والمؤقتات)، والتسوّق (الميزانية)، والرياضة (النتائج). علّمه في السياق الحقيقي عند ظهور الحاجة.

الزمن والنقود والمفاهيم “الحرفية”

لأن مفاهيم الزمن ضعيفة، اشرح متى تقع الأحداث باستخدام علامات دقيقة وملموسة (“بعد الغداء”) وجداول بصرية؛ وتأكد من أن النشاط الذي تسمّيه هو فعلًا آخر نشاط قبل وقت العودة إلى المنزل. Newton ch.7

تمرين 6.1 — تكييف درس رياضيات للصف الثامن عن النسب المئوية

هدف التعلّم: حساب نسبة مئوية من مقدار. سيحلّ الصف 12 سؤالًا في ورقة عمل. رافي لديه متلازمة داون، ويقرأ جملًا بسيطة، ويستخدم آلة حاسبة.

المهمة: صمّم (أ) المقدمة المحسوسة، و(ب) الدعومات، و(ج) تلميحًا ميسِّرًا، و(د) تلميحًا إثرائيًا، و(هـ) كيفية التقييم.

(أ) مشهد تخفيضات من الحياة الواقعية: بطاقات أسعار تُظهر خصم 10% و25% و50%؛ وتقطيع لوح شوكولاتة إلى أعشار وأرباع ونصفين. (ب) مخطط للنسبة المئوية والكسر والعدد العشري على المكتب؛ وآلة حاسبة؛ وشبكة ملوّنة من 100 مربع؛ وإطار جملة “10% of ___ is ” (أي «10% من ___ يساوي »). (ج) التلميح الميسِّر: مثال محلول مع إكمال السطر الأول، أو جدول مملوء جزئيًا، يُقدَّم عندما يتوقف. (د) التلميح الإثرائي: “أيهما أرخص: خصم 25% على 40 جنيهًا إسترلينيًا أم خصم 10% على 30 جنيهًا؟” أو مقارنة متجرين. (هـ) لاحظ كيف يجد 10% من ثلاثة أسعار باستخدام الشبكة والآلة الحاسبة ويشرح اختياراته شفهيًا أو بالإيضاح، وسجّل ذلك على ورقة الدرس. أبقِ على مخرَج الصف الثامن، وقلّل عدد البنود، واستخدم الأدوات. DSi §4.2.1–4.2.2, Rec 25

أهم النقاط

  • القراءة نقطة قوة نسبية: علّمها بالكلمات البصرية والكتب والصور وأغراض حقيقية.
  • اربط القراءة بالكلام؛ واستخدم التقنية في الكتابة.
  • علّم الرياضيات على مستوى الصف بمواد محسوسة ومخططات وآلات حاسبة.
  • علّم المفاهيم المالية لا التقنيات القديمة؛ وقِ المتعلّم من الاستغلال بمستشارين موثوقين.
Core practice · 07

Numeracy in Depth & Everyday Life Skills

Staged procedures for number, measurement, time and money; year-level maths with adjustments; and task-analysed life skills from personal care to travel.

≈ 46 min read9761 words

Why a deep tab on numeracy and life skills

The Literacy tab gives a short overview of mathematics. This tab goes further, because number and everyday living skills are two sides of one goal: a person who can use mathematics and manage daily routines with as little support as possible. The Guidelines link numeracy directly to quality of life. They note that “numeracy development may require explicit planning for people with intellectual disabilities because opportunities to do so vicariously may be limited” (Vicarious learning learning is the incidental learning that most people absorb without being taught). DSi §5.3.3

Two messages run through the sources. First, mathematics is learnable well beyond basic arithmetic when the year-level curriculum is adjusted and tools are used. DSi §4.2.1 Second, independence is built in small, taught steps and “at the pace that is right for them.” Chitty & Dawson ch.10 Neither happens by accident, and both are best taught in the places where the skill will be used.

How to use this tab

Part A covers how number learning develops and the principles for teaching it. Part B gives staged procedures with tables of tools, example tasks and “how to know it is secure”. Part C shows year-level adjustments. Part D applies mathematics to real life. Part E covers daily living skills with task analyses. Part F gives assessment tools. Exercises and takeaways close the tab. Items marked Synthesis are the author’s own synthesis or teaching templates, not quotations from the four sources.

Part A. How number learning develops, and principles for teaching it

What the sources tell us

The sources contain less on number than on language, so it is important to be honest about what is established and what is professional practice.

  • Working memory shapes the maths lesson. “Visual-spatial working memory is a relative strength” and “verbal working memory appears to be a significant weakness, even for those with relatively…” higher ability; the Guidelines say limits of verbal working memory “should be considered in education planning.” DSi §2.2.4 Working memory is the system used to hold a number in mind while doing something with it, which is exactly what mental arithmetic and multi-step word problems demand. Synthesis
  • Aids reduce load. Number lines, calculators, letter charts, grids and diagrams are recommended, and “ready availability of these supports reduces the load on a student’s working memory”; charts can be fixed to the desk or kept in the back of an older student’s workbook. DSi §4.2.2
  • Teaching should start with a check of number understanding. Before adding, “it is useful to check a child’s grasp of numbers.” Newton ch.8
  • Pictures must not distract. If pictures are used in teaching, “they should not be cluttered up with misleading material, particularly when counting.” Concentration may be limited for some activities and “a change of activity may produce a better response.” Newton ch.8
  • Words like “more” and “last” may be read literally. One cannot assume the child will understand terms such as “top of the page”, “first”, “last”, “a lot” or “more” (in the mathematical sense). Newton ch.8 Literal interpretation is therefore a teaching target, not a fault.
  • Tasks are broken into the smallest steps, “perhaps starting with the last stage”, and children “need to learn the next step”; the child’s grasp of each step should be checked. Newton ch.8
  • Results can exceed expectations. Learners who had not shown mastery of simple arithmetic have been reported achieving goals in algebra and trigonometry, supported by calculators as needed. DSi §4.2.1

What the sources do not say

The four sources do not provide a validated developmental sequence of number skills for Down syndrome, age norms for counting, or the results of specific maths programmes. The staged sequence in Part B is built from general mathematics-teaching practice and the strengths and needs profile in the Guidelines. It is a teaching map, not a norm: learners vary widely and may move ahead in one strand while consolidating another. Synthesis

A strengths-based reading of the profile Synthesis

Feature in the profile Implication for maths Teaching response
Visual-spatial memory relatively strong DSi §2.2.4 Number lines, grids, ten-frames, diagrams and graphs are accessible Show structure visually before expecting a spoken explanation
Verbal working memory weak DSi §2.2.4 Long spoken instructions and word problems overload One instruction at a time; write or picture the steps; keep numbers in view
Learning by imitation DSi §5.2.1 Modelling, think-aloud demonstrations and peer partners work Show, then do together, then do alone
Long-term memory good DSi §2.2.4 Routines and procedures once learned are retained Keep a stable method and layout; avoid switching methods
Fine-motor difficulty DSi §2.2.5 Writing numerals and drawing diagrams can be a barrier Number stamps, magnetic digits, large grids, tablet or calculator input
Literal language Newton ch.8 Maths vocabulary can mislead Teach each term with objects, gesture and a picture
Hearing and vision differences DSi §2.2.1 DSi §2.2.2 Small print, faint lines and noisy rooms hide the maths Large, high-contrast materials; seat near the teacher; check hearing and sight

Principles for teaching maths

  1. Plan from the year-level concept. Start from what the class is learning, then adjust. “Appropriate adjustments are then planned”; enabling prompts are “only offered after the learner indicates the need”, and extending prompts provide depth “rather than assigning work from later year levels.” DSi §4.2.1 Learners should have the opportunity to learn the curriculum for their year level, adjusted as necessary. DSi Rec 25 Year-level curriculum with adjustments
  2. Move concrete, then pictorial, then abstract. Handle real objects, then use pictures, ten-frames and diagrams, then use numerals and symbols. Return to the concrete whenever a new idea arrives. Synthesis
  3. Protect working memory. Keep the number line, hundreds chart, number facts card and calculator within reach, and teach the learner to fetch them without being asked. DSi §4.2.2
  4. Teach the calculator as a tool for thinking. Teach when to use it, how to enter numbers, how to check the answer is sensible, and how to read the display. The calculation is done by the tool; the learner decides what to calculate and what the answer means. DSi §4.2.1 Synthesis
  5. Teach the language of maths explicitly. Pair each word with a gesture, picture and object; use the same word each time; check understanding by action, not by “yes”. Newton ch.8
  6. One new idea at a time, with a stable layout. Declutter pages; limit the number of items; use colour consistently for the same job (for instance, tens in blue and ones in red). Newton ch.8 Synthesis
  7. Teach in context. Count the real plates, measure the real ingredients, pay for the real snack. Skills learned only in school can be hard to transfer; the Guidelines note difficulties with transfer for literacy and advise learning in the contexts themselves. DSi §5.3.3
  8. Check understanding by doing and explaining with materials. Written answers may under-represent what is known. Synthesis
  9. Teach concepts, not just techniques that may become outdated. In countries with electronic payment, counting coins matters less than budgeting, saving and spending. DSi §5.3.3
  10. Use errorless and low-error practice, then fade. Arrange tasks so the learner succeeds, then withdraw the prompt gradually; praise the effort and the method. Synthesis

A lesson skeleton that respects working memory

Show the problem on the board with a picture. Say it once, in one short sentence. Let the learner act it out with objects. Write the number sentence beside the picture. Let the learner use the calculator or number line to find the answer. Ask “How do you know?” and accept pointing, showing or telling. End with one real-life use. Synthesis

Part B. Staged teaching procedures

Each stage below has a worked procedure and a table row in the overview. The sequence is a map; a learner may work on two or three stages at once (for instance counting to 10 while learning to read analogue clock hours). Synthesis

Overview: stages, tools, example tasks and security checks Synthesis

Stage Main tools Example task How to know it is secure
1. Counting and one-to-one correspondence Counters, trays, egg cartons, finger sticks, ten-frame “Give me 5 grapes.” Count 8 cars into a box Gives the requested number 4 times in 5 on different days; touches each item once; knows the last number tells “how many”
2. Number recognition and number line Numeral cards, magnetic digits, number line 0 to 20, dice Match numeral 6 to six dots; point to 9 on the line Names and finds numerals to 10 (then 20) in mixed order, in different fonts and in the real world (bus number, price)
3. Quantity comparison Two trays, balance scale, towers of cubes, picture cards “Which has more?” Put the bigger tower next to the smaller Chooses “more”, “less” and “same” correctly with new objects and in a story
4. Place value Base-ten blocks, bundled sticks, place-value mat with colour columns, hundreds chart Show 34 with 3 tens and 4 ones Builds, names and writes two-digit numbers; says which digit is tens
5. Addition and subtraction with tools Counters, number line, ten-frame, calculator, number sentence mat 5 apples and 3 more: how many? Solves new problems with the tool, chooses the right operation, and checks the answer with the calculator
6. Multiplication ideas Arrays, equal groups, skip-counting on a line, calculator 3 plates with 4 biscuits each Builds equal groups and arrays, states the repeated addition and gets the total with a tool
7. Fractions Folded paper, pizza or fraction circles, fraction wall Share a sandwich into halves and quarters Shows half and quarter of shapes and quantities and says why the parts must be equal
8. Measurement Rulers, tape, kitchen scales, jugs, cups Measure the table with hand-spans, then with a ruler Chooses a suitable tool and unit and reads the scale to the nearest mark
9. Time Analogue clock with moveable hands, digital clock, visual timetable, timer app Set the clock to the time of lunch Reads and sets o’clock then half past; links times to the day’s events; reads digital times as on a phone
10. Money Real or realistic coins and notes, price cards, shop role-play, card and phone payment practice Buy a 2 unit snack with a 5 unit note Makes simple purchases, checks a total with a calculator, and knows what “not enough” means
11. Data Real-object graphs, pictograms, block graphs, simple spreadsheet Graph the class’s favourite fruit Sorts, counts, builds a graph and answers “which has the most?”
12. Shape and space Tiles, solid shapes, pegboards, tangrams, maps Find all the circles in the room Names and sorts shapes by features, follows position words and uses a simple plan

Procedure 1: counting and one-to-one correspondence Synthesis

  1. Check the prerequisites. Can the learner attend to a tray of items, reach, grasp and place? Is vision clear for small objects? Place items in a line on a high-contrast mat. DSi §2.2.1
  2. Teach the number words in a rhythm. Say, sign and sing the sequence 1 to 5 together with a sign or gesture for each number; extend to 10 only when 5 is secure. Key-word signing and gestures can support spoken number words. DSi §2.2.3
  3. Teach touching and moving. Use a tray with ten spaces (egg carton). Move each item into a space while saying one number word. Hand-over-hand help first, then pointing, then independent.
  4. Teach “how many” by the last number. After counting, point to the last item and say “five altogether”. Cover the items and ask again. This step is where many learners need repeated practice. Synthesis
  5. Teach “give me”. Ask for 1, 2, 3 items from a larger pile. The learner must stop at the right number; if the pile is large, use a cup to reduce temptation to over-take.
  6. Count different things. Items that move (people), sounds (claps), objects in pictures. Use uncluttered pictures and let the learner mark each counted item with a counter or tick. Newton ch.8
  7. Apply in real tasks. Set the table for four, give out the books, count steps. Link the count to a purpose.
  8. Fade support. Move from hand-over-hand to pointing to a spoken cue to no prompt. Record the level of prompt each time.

Worked example: “Give me 4 grapes”

Place 10 grapes in a bowl and an empty plate with four spaces drawn on it. Say “Four grapes.” Show the numeral 4 and four dots. The learner moves one grape into each space while the adult counts aloud. When all four spaces are filled, the adult says “Four. That is all.” and gives the plate to the learner to eat. Next day, remove the drawn spaces and keep the numeral card. Next week, remove the card. Secure = correct on four days out of five with no card. Synthesis

Procedure 2: number recognition and the number line Synthesis

  1. Start with the learner’s own numbers. Age, house number, bus number, shirt number. Meaningful numerals are recognised faster, in the same way that the child’s own name is the first sight word. Newton ch.8
  2. Match numeral to quantity. Lay out numeral cards 1 to 5 and trays of dots. Match, then sort, then select from a field of three.
  3. Introduce the number line. A strip from 0 to 10 on the desk, with every number in the same colour code (for instance 1 to 5 in blue, 6 to 10 in green). Use a counter as a “frog” that jumps along. Visual-spatial strengths make the line accessible. DSi §2.2.4
  4. Name before and after. “Which number is next? Which number comes before 6?” Use a cover card to hide a number on the line.
  5. Use numerals in context. Lift numbers, microwave timers, price labels, phone keypad, buses.
  6. Write numerals in the best way. Trace, stamp, magnetic digits, a keyboard or a tablet; composing and handwriting are separated. DSi §2.2.5
  7. Extend to 20, then 100 on the hundreds chart. Keep the chart on the desk as a permanent aid. DSi §4.2.2

Procedure 3: comparing quantities Synthesis

  1. Teach the words one at a time. Use “more” first, then “less”, then “same”; each with a picture card and a gesture. Do not assume the child understands “more” in the mathematical sense. Newton ch.8
  2. Line up for comparison. Two rows of objects with matching positions so that the extra items are visible. Use real foods (the learner chooses the bigger pile of crackers).
  3. Contrast with size. Show that a long row can have fewer items than a short row of large items. Count each row to decide.
  4. Move to symbols. Use a “crocodile mouth” picture facing the larger number to introduce greater than and less than; keep the picture in view.
  5. Use ordinal words. First, second, last, using a race with placed counters; link to the visual schedule. Synthesis
  6. Apply. “Who has more stickers?” “Is the bus number bigger than 20?”

Procedure 4: place value Synthesis

  1. Secure 1 to 10 and “10 is one group”. Count ten cubes, snap them into a rod, and call it “one ten”.
  2. Build teen numbers. “One ten and three ones is thirteen.” Use a ten-frame plus counters.
  3. Use colour columns. A place-value mat: tens column blue, ones column red. The digit’s colour matches the column.
  4. Build, say, write. Build 34 with 3 rods and 4 cubes; say “three tens and four ones, thirty-four”; write it by placing digit cards over the mat.
  5. Trade. Ten ones are exchanged for one ten. Practise with real coins of ten units and one unit if the local currency allows.
  6. Link to the hundreds chart. Rows are tens; moving down one row adds ten.
  7. Extend to hundreds and decimals only with the same structure. Decimals follow naturally through money and measurement. Synthesis

Procedure 5: addition and subtraction with tools Synthesis

  1. Tell and act out a story. “Sam has 3 apples. Mum gives him 2 more.” Use real apples.
  2. Combine and count all. Count 3, count 2, push together, count all. Record with the number sentence 3 + 2 = 5 on a mat that shows the objects beside it.
  3. Count on using a number line. Start at 3, make 2 jumps, land on 5. Use a counter on the line.
  4. Introduce the calculator. Press 3, press +, press 2, press =. Compare the display with the counted answer.
  5. Subtraction as take away. Start with 5, hide 2, count what is left; then use a jump back on the line. Introduce “difference” later with two towers side by side.
  6. Teach the key word and the sign together. Plus means “and”; take away means “less”. Attach a picture to each symbol on the page.
  7. Move to bridging 10 with ten-frames. 8 + 5: fill the frame to 10, then add the remaining 3.
  8. Use real problems with a short sentence. Three or fewer words per number idea; write the sentence beside a picture. Reduce the verbal load. DSi §2.2.4
  9. Check with the calculator, then explain in your own way. The learner shows or tells how they know the answer is sensible.

Worked example: 8 + 5 with a ten-frame

Show a ten-frame with 8 counters. Ask “How many more to make ten?” The learner places 2 counters; the frame is full. “We used 2 of the 5. How many are left?” Three. “Ten and three more is thirteen.” Write 8 + 5 = 13, and then press the same numbers on the calculator to confirm. Synthesis

Procedure 6: multiplication ideas Synthesis

  1. Equal groups. Lay out 3 plates with the same number of biscuits on each. Say “3 groups of 2.”
  2. Repeated addition. 2 + 2 + 2 on the number line, three jumps of two.
  3. Arrays. Arrange counters in 3 rows of 4; turn the page to show 4 rows of 3 give the same total.
  4. Skip-count with a rhythm. Count by 2s, 5s and 10s with clapping or stepping; use the hundreds chart to highlight the pattern.
  5. Calculator and table chart. Use a multiplication grid on the desk (a permanent aid) instead of requiring memorisation of all facts. DSi §4.2.2
  6. Link to real tasks. Four people, three biscuits each: how many to buy?
  7. Introduce sharing (division) as the reverse. Share 12 grapes among 4 friends so each has the same.

Procedure 7: fractions Synthesis

  1. Begin with halves and sharing. Share a sandwich between two; the parts must be equal. Cut, compare, overlay.
  2. Fold paper. Fold into halves, then quarters. Colour one part and name it.
  3. Link to real objects. Pizza slices, a chocolate bar, a measuring jug.
  4. Use a fraction wall. A permanent chart showing 1, halves, quarters and eighths aligned. Learners compare by sight, using their visual strength. DSi §2.2.4
  5. Fractions of quantities. Half of 8 counters: share between two plates.
  6. Connect to decimals and percentages through money and sales. 50% off, half price, quarter of a pound (or the local equivalent). Synthesis

Procedure 8: measurement Synthesis

  1. Compare directly. Longer, shorter, heavier, lighter, full, empty, using the two objects side by side.
  2. Use non-standard units. Hand-spans, cubes, cups. Count the units.
  3. Introduce standard units by showing why we need them: my hand-span and yours differ.
  4. Teach the tool. Ruler: line up the zero, place a finger at the end, read the nearest mark. Mark zero in red on a large ruler.
  5. Practise in cooking and craft. Measure flour, cut ribbon, check the height of a plant.
  6. Teach reading scales. Kitchen scales, thermometers and jugs: colour the target line with a marker.
  7. Estimate, then measure. Make it a game; accept any sensible guess.

Procedure 9: time, analogue and digital Synthesis

Time words are abstract, and Newton advises explaining when events occur with accurate, concrete markers and visual timetables. Newton ch.7

  1. Sequence the day first. Use the visual schedule with photographs: morning, lunch, afternoon, home. Before, after and next are taught with the schedule. Newton ch.7
  2. Teach the clock face as a number line bent into a circle. Use a clock with large numerals and a coloured hour hand (short and thick) and minute hand (long and thin).
  3. Hours first. “Lunch is at 12 o’clock.” Set the clock hands, say the time, match to a digital display.
  4. Half past. Show the minute hand at 6; the hour hand is halfway between two numbers.
  5. Quarter past and to. Link to fractions: a quarter of the circle.
  6. Digital time. Teach reading 3:30 on a phone; match with analogue. Digital time is often more useful for daily life. DSi Rec 45
  7. Use timers and alarms. Visual countdown timers, phone alarms and calendar reminders make time visible; the Guidelines recommend everyday tools such as a smartphone calendar. DSi §4.2.2
  8. Teach duration. “Five minutes” is shown with a sand timer or timer app.
  9. Calendar skills. Days of the week with pictures, months with seasonal symbols, a monthly calendar with events marked in colour.

Procedure 10: money Synthesis

The Guidelines state that counting coins and calculating change matter less where payment is electronic, and that concepts such as budgeting, saving, spending, earning interest and borrowing matter most. DSi §5.3.3 Teach both: enough coin and note work to understand value, and strong concept and tool use.

  1. Recognise coins and notes by colour, size and number; sort and match.
  2. Teach value through exchange. “This buys one biscuit; this buys three.” Use real shop play.
  3. Teach the price check. Read the price tag, compare with the money held, decide “enough” or “not enough”.
  4. Pay with a larger note and wait for change. The learner need not calculate change exactly; they should know to wait and check with a calculator or receipt.
  5. Practise electronic payment. Teach card and phone payment, PIN secrecy, checking the screen and the receipt. DSi Rec 45
  6. Introduce a simple budget. Money in, money out, money left; use a three-column chart or spreadsheet. DSi §5.3.3
  7. Teach safety. Never share the PIN; check with a trusted person before a big purchase; “more than one trusted advisor” oversees larger expenditure. DSi Rec 46

Procedure 11 and 12: data, shape and space Synthesis

  1. Sort real objects by one feature (colour), then two (colour and size). Name the groups.
  2. Make an object graph. Each child puts a counter on a mat under their favourite fruit; compare the columns.
  3. Move to pictograms and block graphs. One picture equals one child. Ask “Which has the most? The fewest? How many altogether?”
  4. Use a spreadsheet or app to make a bar chart from the data; the tool removes the drawing barrier. DSi §5.3.3
  5. Shape hunt. Find circles, squares, triangles at home and in the street; name the features (corners, sides).
  6. Build and take apart. Tiles, blocks, tangrams. Copy a model; then make a pattern; then describe it.
  7. Position and direction words (under, next to, between, left, right) taught with the body, then with a map of the classroom or the route to school. Synthesis

Part C. Year-level maths with adjustments

The Guidelines describe planning “from the curriculum materials established for the year level of the class”, with enabling and extending prompts, and caution that assigning later-year work “would lead to boredom in subsequent classes”. DSi §4.2.1 The table below is an illustration of that method across year bands. Year labels differ by country; read them as approximate bands, and adapt the examples to your own curriculum. Synthesis

Adjusting by year band Synthesis

Year band (approx. age) Year-level concept Access adjustment Enabling prompt Extending prompt
Reception and Year 1 (5 to 6) Counting to 20, number bonds to 10, comparing lengths Ten-frames, counters on a tray, large numerals, number line on the desk A ten-frame with some counters already placed “Can you find two different ways to make 7?”
Year 2 (6 to 7) Two-digit numbers, adding and subtracting within 20, simple money Place-value mat in colour, base-ten blocks, hundreds chart, real coins A worked example with the first step done “Make 35 in two different ways using tens and ones.”
Years 3 and 4 (7 to 9) Multiplication facts, fractions, time to the minute, measurement Multiplication grid, fraction wall, clock with coloured hands, calculator for checking A partly filled array to complete “If 4 friends share 12 grapes, then 6 friends share 12 grapes. What changes?”
Years 5 and 6 (9 to 11) Decimals, percentages, area and perimeter, averages, graphs Tiled grids for area, real-life price tags, calculator for computation, graph template A table with the first row completed “Which shop has the cheaper offer, 25% off 40 or 10% off 30?”
Years 7 and 8 (11 to 13) Ratio, proportion, negative numbers, simple algebra, angle Number line to show negatives, balance-scale model for equations, physical angle measurers, calculator A flow diagram showing the first step “Make up your own equation puzzle for a friend.”
Years 9 and 10 (13 to 15) Linear equations, Pythagoras, probability, financial maths Algebra tiles, graph-plotting software, probability spinners, spreadsheet for budgets A model solution with one line missing “Plan a class trip budget and test what happens if prices rise.”
Years 11 and 12 (15 to 18) Applied maths for life: budgets, loans, statistics, trigonometry for those who choose it Spreadsheet templates, banking apps, calculators, real data A checklist of the steps in the task “Compare two phone plans and justify your choice.”

Beyond basic arithmetic

The Guidelines cite reports of learners who had not demonstrated simple arithmetic achieving goals in algebra and trigonometry, supported by calculators as needed (Faragher, 2014; Monari Martinez, 1998; Monari Martinez & Pellegrini, 2010). Learners should not be held back at counting before they meet interesting year-level ideas. DSi §4.2.1

Adjustment types in maths Synthesis

The Guidelines list four ways to make the curriculum accessible, which apply naturally to maths. DSi §4.2.1

Adjustment Maths example
Modification (changing how the learner responds) Point to the answer, build with blocks or use a calculator instead of writing every working line
Substitution Use a talking calculator or enlarged display instead of small print
Omission Leave out very complex multi-step problems while keeping the core concept
Compensation Teach a related life skill (checking change) to cover an area of difficulty
Same activity, less of it Five well-chosen questions instead of twenty; the same concept, fewer items

Part D. Maths in real life

“Numeracy” in the Guidelines is the use of mathematics in life contexts, and it is linked with quality of life. DSi §5.3.3 Real tasks supply meaning, motivation and a reason to practise. Every worked example below uses a fictional person and plausible figures; replace the amounts and currency with your own. Synthesis

Shopping Synthesis

Component Support Maths involved
Plan the list Photo list or app with pictures Counting items, sorting by aisle
Check money Wallet card, budget limit written Comparing quantities
Choose items Price cards; “is it more or less than my limit?” Comparing prices, rounding
Pay Card or cash; wait for receipt Money value, change
Check receipt Tick against the list Matching, totals

Worked example: a snack shop trip

Amira has 10 units. She wants a drink (3 units), a sandwich (4 units) and a piece of fruit (2 units). Step 1: she lays three price cards on the mat. Step 2: she adds with the calculator: 3 + 4 + 2 = 9. Step 3: she compares 9 with 10: “enough, with 1 left”. Step 4: she pays and checks the receipt. Enabling prompt: the calculator already open with 3 + 4 entered. Extending prompt: “She also wants a 2-unit biscuit. Is there enough? What could she swap?” Synthesis

Cooking Synthesis

Component Support Maths involved

Worked example: pancakes for four

The recipe makes 2 pancakes with 1 cup of flour. For 4 people, two pancakes each: the learner needs 8 pancakes, which is 4 times the recipe. A table is on the card: 2 pancakes, 1 cup; 4 pancakes, 2 cups; 8 pancakes, 4 cups. The learner reads across to find 4 cups and uses a marked jug to measure, counting each cup into the bowl aloud and placing a counter in a tray for each. Enabling prompt: the row already highlighted. Extending prompt: “We only have 3 cups of flour. How many pancakes can we make?” Synthesis

Travel Synthesis

Component Support Maths involved
Read the timetable Highlighted row, phone app Digital time, ordering
Plan the route Picture map, numbered stops Counting, sequence
Pay the fare Travel card, top-up Money, budget
Check arrival Phone alarm, reminders Duration, time to go

Worked example: catching the 10:15 bus

The class trip leaves school at 9:30. The bus comes at 10:15 and the walk takes 15 minutes. When must Daniel leave? The learner counts back on a clock face: 15 minutes before 10:15 is 10:00. He sets his phone alarm for 9:55 so that he leaves with five minutes spare. Enabling prompt: a clock with the bus time marked. Extending prompt: “What if the walk takes 25 minutes?” Synthesis

Budgeting Synthesis

The Guidelines emphasise teaching concepts rather than outdated techniques, and using tools such as online banking and spreadsheets that remove the calculation barrier. Trusted advisers should oversee larger expenditure. DSi §5.3.3 DSi Rec 46

Component Support Maths involved
Income Pay slip with highlighted total Reading numbers, addition
Must-pay costs Colour-coded boxes: rent, food, phone Addition
Choose costs Picture cards for wants Comparing, choosing
Saving Goal chart with a picture of the item Repeated addition, fractions
Review Monthly check with a trusted adviser Subtraction, graphs

Worked example: saving for headphones

Tariq earns 60 units a week at his work placement. His must-pay column is 25 (travel and phone). He chooses 15 for leisure. The rest, 20, goes to saving. The headphones cost 80. He draws four boxes on a goal chart and colours one each week. After four weeks the chart is full. A spreadsheet row shows the same, and an app shows 20, 40, 60, 80. Enabling prompt: columns already labelled. Extending prompt: “If he saves 25 a week, how many weeks does he save?” Synthesis

Part E. Everyday life skills

Independence is built in small steps and at the right pace. Chitty advises that “supporting your child to become more independent is something that has to be done at the pace that is right for them”, with early involvement in home tasks (for instance talking about the washing in the early teens) and conversation about cooking and healthy eating. Chitty & Dawson ch.10 Newton’s guidance on teaching fits all of the areas below: break the task into the smallest steps, check the child’s grasp of each, start from the last step if helpful, and use simple wording the child can learn to say alongside the action, such as “Hold, over and push through” for buttons. Newton ch.8

Support need, not diagnosis, sets the starting point

Newton cautions against overemphasis on self-care skills before school entry: they are “not skills that are necessary to start with”; children “learn quickly from other children; children with Down’s syndrome often find copying very easy.” Newton ch.8 This is a reminder to avoid delaying inclusion until skills are perfect. Newton ch.8

Principles for teaching life skills Synthesis

  1. Choose a skill the person wants or needs now. Motivation is the best reinforcer; ask the learner and the family. Reinforcement
  2. Do a task analysis. Break the skill into observable steps, in the order they happen. Task analysis
  3. Assess the baseline. Watch the person try the whole task; mark each step as independent, verbal prompt, gesture, or physical help.
  4. Decide the teaching order. Forward chaining teaches step one first. Backward chaining teaches the last step first so the person finishes and succeeds, then adds earlier steps. Newton recommends teaching “the last step first”, for example putting on trousers. Newton ch.8
  5. Use the least intrusive prompt that works. Order: independent, visual or gesture cue, verbal cue, model, partial physical, full physical. Start with the least that gives success.
  6. Use visual supports. Photo or picture sequence cards; keep the same order every time. Visual schedule / timetable
  7. Teach the same way in every place. Home, school, community staff use the same steps and words, so that learning generalises.
  8. Reinforce success immediately, then fade the reinforcement towards natural consequences (the toast is warm; the shoes are on; the bus arrives).
  9. Fade support systematically. Move one level down the prompt hierarchy once the person succeeds on three consecutive attempts; go back up if errors rise.
  10. Practise in real situations and with different people, rather than only role play. DSi §5.3.3

Fading ladder

Physical help, then partial physical help, then model, then verbal prompt, then gesture, then picture cue, then none. Record the level every session. A skill is secure when it is independent on 80 percent of opportunities across three settings and two people for two weeks. The 80 percent criterion is a practical suggestion, not a standard from the sources. Synthesis

Generalisation across settings Synthesis

The Guidelines note difficulties in transferring strategies learnt in school to other contexts, and suggest teaching in the contexts themselves. DSi §5.3.3 Plan generalisation from the start.

Strategy Example
Same sequence everywhere The photo card for handwashing is on the wall at home and school
Train in the real place Teach the bus journey on the actual bus
Vary people A friend, sibling and teaching assistant each take a turn as helper
Vary materials Use two or three kinds of tap, toaster or bag
Share the plan A communication book or app sent between home and school
Check later Re-test the skill after a break (holiday)

DSi §2.2.5 Skin, hair and body-care routines are also health routines. Personal care in adolescence includes menstrual hygiene: “girls who are independent with toileting are likely to manage their menstrual hygiene”, though they may not indicate pain or understand mood changes. 2. Dressing

Newton recommends teaching dressing steps by starting with the last step, and teaching simple wording to accompany actions. Newton ch.8

Component step (pulling on trousers) Prompt Adaptation How to fade
Lay trousers front-up Photo Mark the front with a sticker or tag Remove sticker after success
Sit on a chair or bed Gesture Seat with back support Stand later
Put one leg in, then the other Verbal “one, two” Elastic-waist trousers Remove verbal
Pull to the knees Gesture Loop on waistband Remove loop
Stand and pull to the waist Model Mirror Fade model
Fasten (button, zip, hook) “Hold, over and push through” Large buttons, zip pull ring, magnetic closures Return to standard fastening

Backward-chaining example: the helper completes everything except the final pull from the knee to the waist. The learner does that last step and gets praise. Next session the learner does “pull to the knees” and the last step, and so on until all steps are independent. Newton ch.8

Further points: label clothes, choose clothes that are “easy to remove for going to the toilet”, and avoid fiddly fastenings at first. Newton ch.8 Teach choosing clothes for weather and occasion with a picture weather board; teach back-to-front and inside-out checks with a mirror and a tag-at-the-back rule. Synthesis

3. Toileting and toilet hygiene

Toilet training “can take a little longer to establish” and “a consistent routine often helps”, such as taking the child to the toilet at the same times each day. Chitty & Dawson ch.3 A regular toilet may be too high, so a footstool helps. Chitty & Dawson ch.7 Check with a health professional if there is constipation, continence difficulty or pain. Synthesis

Component step Prompt Adaptation How to fade

Go to the toilet Visual schedule at set times Clear route; toilet door photo Fade the schedule to natural cues
Lower clothing Photo sequence Elastic waists; avoid dungarees Newton ch.8 Fade photo

Use paper, front to back Model; picture card Pre-measured paper squares (3 squares) Remove card
Flush Verbal Large flush button Fade

Wash and dry hands As personal care Soap and towel at reachable height Fade

Privacy and dignity: teach that toilet and personal care are private, who may help and when, and that “no” is allowed. This links to the personal safety unit below. Synthesis For menstruation, prepare in advance with a picture book, a practice kit and a bag with a spare pad in the school bag. DSi §5.2.2 Synthesis

4. Meal preparation: a full task analysis

Teaching a simple hot meal is a good test of many skills at once: sequence, safety, measuring, timing, and hygiene. Chitty notes that families can begin by talking about cooking and choosing the right balance of food. Chitty & Dawson ch.10

Task analysis: making a cheese toastie safely

  1. Wash hands. 2. Collect bread, cheese, butter, plate, toaster or sandwich maker, knife (blunt). 3. Butter two slices. 4. Place cheese on one slice. 5. Put the second slice on top, butter side out. 6. Switch the sandwich maker on and check the light. 7. Place the sandwich inside and close the lid. 8. Set the timer for 4 minutes. 9. Wait at the table; do not touch the hot metal. 10. When the timer sounds, switch off at the wall. 11. Lift the sandwich out with a wooden spatula. 12. Put on a plate; wait two minutes to cool. 13. Cut in half. 14. Eat. 15. Wash up and put away. Synthesis
Component step group Prompt Adaptation How to fade
Hygiene and set-up (steps 1 to 2) Photo card of ingredients Fixed place for each item; tray Remove photos item by item
Preparation (steps 3 to 5) Model; verbal cue Non-slip mat; spreading knife with a thick handle Fade model to verbal
Cooking (steps 6 to 10) Visual timer; safety card “hot” Timer with a loud alarm; heat-proof gloves Keep the timer; fade other cues
Serving and cleaning (steps 11 to 15) Photo sequence Wipe-down checklist One card for the whole routine

Backward-chaining example for the toastie Newton ch.8 Synthesis

  1. Session 1. The helper does steps 1 to 14; the learner does step 15 (wash up and put away) and is praised. Eating the toastie is the natural reward.
  2. Session 2. The helper does steps 1 to 13; the learner cuts the toastie in half (step 13) and then does steps 14 and 15.
  3. Session 3. The helper does steps 1 to 12; the learner does 12 to 15.
  4. Continue adding one earlier step at a time as the later steps become independent.
  5. Reach step 1 when the whole sequence is independent; fade the photo card and the timer cue last.
  6. Generalise. Make the toastie at home, in the school kitchen and at a friend’s house, with two different machines.

Safety: teach “hot”, “sharp” and “switch off” as fixed phrases with a picture; keep a cooking safety card by the cooker; and plan around fine-motor and balance needs with an occupational therapist where needed. Choose healthy foods using a plate picture; link to health tab advice on diet and weight. Synthesis

6. Travel training and road safety

Teach in stages and in the real environment. Travel training combines orientation, road safety, time-telling, money, communication and personal safety. Mobility benefits were designed for those “who can walk but need someone with them when out of doors”, which is a reminder that some people will need supervision for part of the route. Newton ch.10 (That passage describes UK allowances of its time; check current rules.) Synthesis

Component step Prompt Adaptation How to fade
Know home address and a trusted contact Wallet card with photo ID card with name, address and an emergency phone number Practise saying it
Walk a short, known route with an adult Model Landmark photo cards Adult drops back behind
Stop at the kerb “Stop. Look. Listen. Think.” Painted line at the kerb; practice crossing Verbal to gesture to none
Cross at a safe place Model; verbal Use pedestrian crossings and signals Fade the model
Follow the route by landmarks Photo sequence Phone map with a route line Fade photos
Take the bus or train Ticket card; route number card Travel card; app showing stops; alarm for “get off” stop Support from behind, then no support
Ask for help Script card: “Please can you help me?” Practise with a safe helper (driver, uniformed staff) Fade the card
Deal with change (diversion, delay) “What if” cards Phone call to trusted contact Fade

Travel training steps (an outline) Synthesis

  1. Task-analyse the journey with the learner and family, and walk it yourself, noting hazards.
  2. Teach safety skills first (kerb, crossing, stranger, asking for help) near home.
  3. Accompany the learner, who leads; you only prompt.
  4. Shadow at a distance; the learner travels while you follow unseen, ready to help.
  5. Travel alone with check-ins by phone; the family knows the time of arrival.
  6. Review with photos of the route and stops; plan for changes.
  7. Re-check after a break or a route change.

Hearing and vision matter for road safety. Hearing loss is common and fluctuates, and vision may be reduced even with spectacles, so confirm the learner can hear traffic and see signals. DSi §2.2.1 DSi §2.2.2

The Guidelines recommend that adults be assisted to learn to use devices such as smartphones and computer applications where they are in use by the general community, and note the calendar app as a classroom support. DSi Rec 45 DSi §4.2.2

Part F. Assessment and tracking

Principles Synthesis

  • Assess by doing in real settings, not only on paper.
  • Record the level of prompt as well as correct or incorrect.
  • Record generalisation (where, with whom, with what).
  • Share records with the learner, using pictures and ticks, so they see their own progress.
  • Link to the IEP and review at least each term. DSi Rec 27

Maths checklist (tick when secure)

Life-skills checklist (tick when independent in two settings)

Skills-tracking table template Synthesis

Copy this table for each skill. Prompt levels: I = independent, V = verbal, G = gesture or picture, M = model, P = physical. Setting codes: H = home, S = school, C = community.

Date Skill and step Setting Helper Prompt level Correct (Y/N) Notes and next step

Summary line to complete each term: Skill __ Baseline _ Current Settings secure Next target Review date ___.

Exercises

Exercise 18.1 — Plan a counting session

Jamal (age 6) counts to 10 by rote but when asked for five blocks he usually grabs a handful. Plan a 10-minute session to teach “give me five”, using the principles in Procedure 1.

The problem is one-to-one correspondence and stopping at the target, not rote counting. Use an egg carton or a tray with five drawn spaces, a pile of ten blocks and a numeral 5 card. (1) Adult models moving one block into each space while counting aloud. (2) Jamal moves with hand-over-hand help, then alone, saying one number per block. (3) Adult says “five altogether” pointing to the last block. (4) Ask “Give me five” from the pile; the tray limits the grab. (5) Repeat with 3 and 4. (6) End with a real task: give out five biscuits. Record prompt level. Fade the tray next session, and then the numeral card. Secure when correct on four days of five without the tray. Synthesis Newton ch.8

Exercise 18.2 — Adjust a Year 4 lesson on time

The class objective is “read and write time to the nearest minute on analogue and digital clocks”. Zara has Down syndrome, reads simple words and uses a visual timetable. Design the access adjustment, an enabling prompt, an extending prompt and an assessment.

Keep the year-level objective. Access: a clock with a coloured hour hand and minute hand and large numerals, a minutes strip showing 5, 10, 15 and so on around the dial, a digital display beside it, and her own visual timetable. Reduce the number of items to five well-chosen times, starting with her own school-day events. Enabling prompt (only when she signals need): a worked example with the hour already set, or a partly completed table. Extending prompt: “School ends at 3:15. Lunch is 2 hours and 15 minutes earlier. What time is lunch?” using the clock to count back. Assessment: she sets the clock to five times related to her day and says or points to what happens then; record on the lesson sheet; check that the digital time matches. DSi §4.2.1 Newton ch.7 Synthesis

Exercise 18.3 — Task analysis and backward chaining

Choose a skill (such as making a bowl of cereal and clearing up). Write a task analysis with at least eight steps, and show the first three sessions of a backward-chaining plan.

Example task analysis: 1 wash hands; 2 collect bowl, spoon, cereal, milk; 3 put the bowl on the mat; 4 pour cereal to the line; 5 close the cereal box; 6 pour milk to the line; 7 close the milk and return it to the fridge; 8 sit and eat; 9 carry the bowl to the sink; 10 rinse and put in the rack. Backward chaining: Session 1, the helper does steps 1 to 9 and the learner does step 10 with praise. Session 2, the learner does steps 9 and 10. Session 3, the learner does steps 8 to 10 (eating naturally leads into clearing). Continue until step 1. Record the prompt level at each step. Teach in the kitchen where it will be used, with the same photo card at home and school. Newton ch.8 Synthesis

Exercise 18.4 — Real-life budgeting problem

Lina has 50 units a week. She must pay 20 for travel and phone. She wants to save for a bag that costs 60 and still have some spending money. Build a plan she could follow, using a tool, and suggest an enabling and an extending prompt.

Money left after must-pay costs: 50 - 20 = 30. If she saves 15 and spends 15, she needs 60 / 15 = 4 weeks. Show this on a spreadsheet or a goal chart with four boxes (one coloured per week), using the calculator to check each step. If she saves 10, she needs 6 weeks. A trusted adult reviews the plan monthly, and she does not share her PIN. Enabling prompt: the first row (50, 20, 30) already filled. Extending prompt: “What if the bag is on sale for 45? When can she buy it?” Concepts (budgeting, saving, choosing) matter more than coin handling. DSi §5.3.3 DSi Rec 46 Synthesis

Exercise 18.5 — Travel training plan

Omar (age 16) wants to travel to his weekend sports club by bus, a route of three stops. Outline how you would teach the journey and keep him safe, including generalisation.

Task-analyse: leave the house, walk to the stop, cross the road safely, check the route number card, wait, board and tap the travel card, watch the stops or use the app alarm, press the bell, get off, walk to the club. Teach crossing and asking-for-help scripts near home first. Accompany him on the real route several times, with Omar leading; then shadow from a distance; then travel alone with a phone check-in on arrival. Check hearing and vision for traffic and signals. Give him a wallet card with his name, address and trusted contact, and rehearse “what if the bus doesn’t come?”. Use the same photo sequence at home and school; practise at different times of day and with different helpers; review after the first month and after any route change. Newton ch.10 DSi §2.2.2 DSi Rec 45 Synthesis

Exercise 18.6 — Apply the fading ladder

Sana is learning to use the washing machine. Over three weeks the record shows: Week 1: physical help for two steps; Week 2: model and verbal for four steps; Week 3: independent on six of eight steps, with two errors at choosing the programme. What should you do next?

Progress is good: prompts have faded from physical to model to verbal. Keep the supports that work for the two weak steps and make the programme choice easier: put a coloured sticker on the correct dial setting and a matching dot on a photo card, and return briefly to a gesture prompt for that step only. Keep fading the others, and track with the table template. When she is independent on eight of eight over three sessions, test in a different setting (a relative’s machine or the school laundry) and with a different helper, then remove the sticker last. Synthesis

Key takeaways

  • Number and life skills are best taught in small, visible steps, with concrete materials first, then pictures, then symbols. Synthesis
  • Visual-spatial strengths and verbal working-memory limits shape the lesson: show it, say less, and keep number lines, charts and calculators within reach. DSi §2.2.4 DSi §4.2.2
  • Teach the year-level concept with adjustments, using enabling and extending prompts, rather than waiting for basic arithmetic to be perfect. DSi §4.2.1
  • Teach the language of maths, because “more”, “last” and “top” may be taken literally. Newton ch.8
  • Use real contexts (shopping, cooking, travel, budgeting) and teach concepts such as budgeting and saving, with tools and trusted advisers to guard against financial abuse. DSi §5.3.3 DSi Rec 46
  • Task analysis and backward chaining make daily skills teachable; start from the last step so the learner finishes successfully. Newton ch.8
  • Use the least intrusive prompt that works and fade it on a record, aiming for independence in more than one setting. Synthesis
  • Plan for generalisation: same steps, in real places, with different people. DSi §5.3.3
  • Track progress with checklists and a skills table, and share it with the learner and family. Synthesis
الممارسة الأساسية · 07

الحساب بعمق ومهارات الحياة اليومية

إجراءات متدرجة للعدد والقياس والزمن والمال، ورياضيات على مستوى الصف مع التعديلات، ومهارات حياتية محلّلة المهام من العناية الشخصية إلى التنقل.

≈ 44 دقيقة قراءة9324 كلمة

لماذا تبويب معمّق عن الحساب والمهارات الحياتية

يقدّم تبويب القراءة والكتابة لمحة موجزة عن الرياضيات. أما هذا التبويب فيمضي أبعد، لأن العدد ومهارات المعيشة اليومية وجهان لهدف واحد: شخص يستطيع استخدام الرياضيات وإدارة روتينه اليومي بأقل قدر ممكن من الدعم. وتربط الإرشادات الحسابَ مباشرةً بجودة الحياة. فهي تلاحظ أن “تنمية المهارات الحسابية قد تتطلّب تخطيطًا صريحًا لدى الأشخاص ذوي الإعاقة الفكرية لأن فرص التعلّم بذلك عن طريق غير مباشر قد تكون محدودة” (والتعلّم غير المباشر هو التعلّم العرضي الذي يمتصّه معظم الناس دون أن يُعلَّموه). DSi §5.3.3

تتكرّر في المصادر رسالتان. الأولى أن الرياضيات قابلة للتعلّم إلى ما هو أبعد بكثير من الحساب الأساسي متى جرى تعديل منهج الصف واستُخدمت الأدوات. DSi §4.2.1 والثانية أن الاستقلالية تُبنى بخطوات صغيرة مُعلَّمة و“بالوتيرة المناسبة لهم”. Chitty & Dawson ch.10 ولا يحدث أيٌّ من الأمرين مصادفةً، وأفضل ما يُدرَّسان في الأماكن التي ستُستخدم فيها المهارة.

كيف تستخدم هذا التبويب

يتناول الجزء (أ) كيف ينمو تعلّم العدد ومبادئ تدريسه. ويقدّم الجزء (ب) إجراءات مرحلية مع جداول الأدوات والمهام النموذجية و“كيف تعرف أن المهارة راسخة”. ويعرض الجزء (ج) تعديلات منهج الصف. ويطبّق الجزء (د) الرياضيات في الحياة الواقعية. ويتناول الجزء (هـ) مهارات المعيشة اليومية مع تحليلات للمهام. ويقدّم الجزء (و) أدوات التقييم. وتختتم التمارين وأهم النقاط التبويب. والبنود الموسومة بـ تركيب مهني هي تركيب المؤلف الخاص أو قوالب تدريسية، وليست اقتباسات من المصادر الأربعة.

الجزء (أ). كيف ينمو تعلّم العدد، ومبادئ تدريسه

ما تقوله لنا المصادر

تحتوي المصادر على معلومات عن العدد أقلّ مما تحتويه عن اللغة، ولذلك من المهم الصراحة في ما هو مثبَت وما هو ممارسة مهنية.

  • الذاكرة العاملة تشكّل درس الرياضيات. “الذاكرة العاملة البصرية المكانية نقطة قوة نسبية” و“الذاكرة العاملة اللفظية تبدو نقطة ضعف كبيرة، حتى لدى من لديهم قدرة أعلى نسبيًا…”؛ وتقول الإرشادات إن حدود الذاكرة العاملة اللفظية “ينبغي أخذها في الاعتبار عند التخطيط التربوي”. DSi §2.2.4 والذاكرة العاملة هي النظام المستخدم لإبقاء عدد في الذهن أثناء إجراء عملية عليه، وهذا بالضبط ما يتطلبه الحساب الذهني ومسائل الكلمات متعددة الخطوات. تركيب مهني
